In recent years, they have also been shown to be effective architectures for other modalities. One particular modality of interest is computer vision (Chen et al., 2020a; Touvron et al., 2020); in particular, Dosovitskiy et al. (2020) showed that transformers can outperform CNNs in the high-data regime on standard object recognition benchmarks such as ImageNet and CIFAR. Furthermore, transformers have also been used for prediction tasks over protein sequences (Jumper et al., 2021; Rao et al., 2021), reinforcement learning (Parisotto et al., 2020), and imitation learning (Abramson et al., 2020). Work speciﬁcally tackling multimodal tasks include Kaiser et al. (2017), who showed a single model could learn a variety of multimodal tasks with an attention architecture. Recent work has utilized transformers for multimodal predictive tasks, such as images and text in ViLBERT (Lu et al., 2019) and CLIP (Radford et al., 2021); these approaches generally use two distinct transformers to embed images and text. Lu et al. (2020) applies ViLBERT to train a single model for a variety of combined vision and language tasks. Recent work from OpenAI (Goh et al., 2021) ﬁnds that some neurons learned by CLIP are activated by a particular semantic concept, regardless of if the concept is pre- sented in language or picture form. Our work is most similar to DALL-E (Ramesh et al., 2021), which uses a single transformer to embed both the image and text modalities, which we consider to be generating a “universal latent space” that projects any type of input into a single latent space. Such a latent space would be useful for a model that could learn from many sources of supervision. 4.2 Transformers in transfer settings There are also many works looking at transformers speciﬁcally in the context of in-modality trans- fer, such as ViT for vision (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020), T5 for language (Raffel et al., 2019), and UDSMProt for protein sequences (Strodthoff et al., 2020). CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) showed that training on text in addition to images could allow for zero-shot classiﬁcation via providing down- stream labels as text. Hernandez et al. (2021) do a thorough investigation of transfer with language pretraining, notably showing transfer from English to Python, which they consider to be reasonably distanced from English; many works have also looked at transferring from one langauge to another (Artetxe et al., 2019; Ponti et al., 2019). Similar to our work, Papadimitriou & Jurafsky (2020) 13investigate transfer for LSTMs between modalities including code, different languages, and music, ﬁnding that pretraining on “non-linguistic data with latent structure” can transfer to language, ﬁnd- ing grammatical structure in a modality to be important, although we generally investigate the other direction and explore more distanced modalities. Kiela et al. (2019) make similar observations for aligning representation spaces of language and vision. Li et al. (2020) pretrain on a referential com- munication game where an emergent learned language is used to transfer to NLP tasks. Wu et al. (2021) found explicitly pretraining computational primitives to transfer to mathematics tasks. 4.3 Pretraining and ﬁnetuning of transformer models A common trend in deep learning models is to ﬁrst train a large model on an unsupervised objective on a large dataset (Dai & Le, 2015; Radford et al., 2018) and then ﬁnetune on a small downstream dataset (e.g., by freezing the model and only ﬁnetuing the output layer). A common method used to ﬁnetune transformers are adapter networks (Rebufﬁ et al., 2017; Houlsby et al., 2019), which add a fully connected residual block for each unique downstream task and also ﬁnetune the layer norm parameters. For simplicity, we do not add the full adapter block but only train the layer norm parameters, reducing the number of parameters we consider. These techniques used are similar to prior approaches such as FiLM (Perez et al., 2018) and self-modulation (Chen et al., 2018). A recent direction of research has explored learning prompt templates for large models (Shin et al., 2020) that simply require forward passes over the transformer. Unlike these works, we consider ﬁnetuning on one modality (language) and ﬁnetuning on others, whereas prior work investigates ﬁnetuning on the same modality as the pretraining task. Another interesting related work, although not investigating transformers, by Frankle et al. (2020) ﬁnd randomly initialized CNNs, which only train the batchnorm afﬁne parameters, to work well on CIFAR-10. Their numbers are stronger than ours on CIFAR-10, but include signiﬁcantly more inductive bias via a convolutional architecture, so the main takeaway is slightly more relevant towards image tasks rather than arbitrary sequences. 4.4 Self-attention layers as optimization steps The nature of computation performed by self-attention layers has also been explored by other related works. Bai et al. (2019) show that a single transformer self-attention block can be trained to perform an optimization step towards ﬁnding a stationary point, representing the solution to the task. Ram- sauer et al. (2020) show that the self-attention layer is a gradient step in a Hopﬁeld network with a learning rate of 1, hinting that transformers are capable of storing and retrieving a large amount of patterns with an implicit energy function. An interesting discussion from Goyal & Bengio (2020) points out a connection in viewing the key-value queries used in attention as similar to function sig- natures in computer programming: the key maps the input to a type (e.g., ﬂoat) and the value maps the input to its value (e.g., 3.14), and if the type matches the function signature, the function can be applied to the value – this may be particularly relevant when we consider using a single self-attention layer applied to different modalities, as the modality may be embedded in the type. 4.5 Global workspace theory A common technique for evaluating the embeddings learned by an unsupervised model is to train a linear layer on top of the embeddings for a downstream task (Donahue et al., 2016; Oord et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020b), which is reasonable when you ﬁnetune on the same modality as the pretrained one. However, when ﬁnetuning on a different modality, as in our setting, we have to reframe this notion of generalizable embedding quality – instead of only ﬁnetuning the output layer, we also want to ﬁnetune the input layer, and instead evaluate the ability of the frozen intermediate model to perform generalizable computation. This is reminiscent of Global Workspace Theory (Baars, 1993), which revolves around the notion that there is a “blackboard” that different parts of the brain send data to; we might consider the frozen language model as being a blackboard in this setting. Language might also be a natural choice of model for this blackboard, as there are hypotheses that language may serve as a good multipurpose high-level representation for cognitive behavior and conscious planning (Andreas et al., 2017; Goyal & Bengio, 2020). 144.6 Reservoir computing Similarly to the FPT setup and Global Workspace Theory, in reservoir computing (Tanaka et al., 2019) and echo state networks (Jaeger, 2001; Jaeger & Haas, 2004), a random recurrent network is frozen and only the output readout layer is trained. These models are very fast to train, using a similar setup as in Section 3.9, because the activations of the recurrent network can be cached and it is unnecessary to backpropagate over time. Somewhat differently to the FPT architecture, echo state networks are recurrent and thus feed back into themselves, which allows the outputs of the random frozen network to modulate future inputs. Unlike echo state networks, we also notably ﬁnetune the input and positional embeddings, which allow the inputs to the frozen network to adapt to a particular modality/for a query to the frozen network to be learned. Echo state networks are also similar to the perspective of self-attention applying a data-dependent ﬁlter to the inputs, as opposed to 1D convolutions, which are ﬁxed ﬁlters regardless of the input modality. 5 Conclusion We proposed transferring a pretrained transformer language model for downstream tasks in non- language modalities. Through extensive empirical evaluation, we showed that these models could achieve performance competitive with transformers fully trained on the downstream task without having to ﬁnetune the self-attention and feedforward layers, relying solely on frozen parameters from the language model to perform the bulk of the computation. We believe this work can serve as the foundation for future work investigating transfer between modalities. In future, we are interested in investigating the use of other data-rich modalities (e.g., vision) or a hybrid of multiple domains being used to provide the necessary substrate for pretraining a universal computational engine. It would also be interesting to explore frozen pretrained models for tasks beyond predictive modeling, such as reinforcement learning (Abramson et al., 2020). We note that a limitation of our analysis in that we analyze speciﬁc models on a restricted set of tasks. More investigation can highlight whether or not similar behavior occurs for other models on other tasks. For instance, in Section 3.14, we ﬁnd the architecture can have a signiﬁcant impact on results. As training regimes for these models evolve, performing similar experiments may yield different results, and we are excited for more research in this direction. For high stakes applications in the real-world, there are potential concerns with transfer of harmful biases from one modality to one another using pretrained transformer models trained on vast quan- tities of unlabeled, uncurated datasets (Sheng et al., 2019; Bender et al., 2021). Mitigating these biases is an active area of research (Grover et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2020). Conversely, there are also potential upsides with FPT models being able to better exploit representative datasets from one or more modalities, which merit future investigation as well. B Background on Transformers In this section, we give a description of the transformer architecture used in our experiments, namely the GPT-2 architecture (Radford et al., 2019). B.1 Self-Attention The main subcomponent of the transformer architecture is the self-attention layer, which takes in l input tokens and outputs loutput tokens, both of dimensionndim. Each input token xi is mapped by linear transformations Q, K, and V – denoting query, key, and values, respectively – intoqi, ki, and vi. Both qi and ki have dimension dk, and vi has dimension dv. To generate the output token yi, dot products are calculated between query qi and keys kj, and fed into a softmax operation to generate weights wi ∈[0,1] (in practice, a scaling temperature factor of 1√dk is used to reduce the sharpness of the softmax). Then, the weights are used to generate yi as a weighted sum of all the values, i.e.: yi = l∑ j=1 exp(q⊤ i kj) ∑l k=1 exp(q⊤ i kk) vj (1) This is extended to multi-head attention over nheads heads by doing the above procedure nheads times, and then concatenating. To recover the original dimension the concatenated vector (of di- mension dvnheads) is multiplied by a projection matrix Wproj ∈Rdvnheads×ndim . GPT-2 applies a causal mask to its inputs, i.e. the output token i is only allowed to attend to the input tokens j ≤i, which changes the upper bounds of the sums in Equation 1 toiinstead of l. This allows for unsupervised pretraining methods like language modeling (see Appendix B.4). A residual connection is used to connect the inputs with the outputs of the attention layer. Then, in the rest of the transformer block, a two-layer MLP is used, conventionally projecting the dimension upwards to 4 ·ndim for the inner dimension and using the GELU activation function (Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2016). Another residual connection is used to connect the outputs of the MLP with the previous outputs of the attention layer. This forms the basis of the transformer block. As it preserves the dimension ndim, multiple blocks can be learned and stacked on top of each other nlayers times, before feeding the ﬁnal hidden states to the output layer. In our work, we only use the output of the last hidden state for classiﬁcation, although in principle other methods are reasonable. B.2 Positional Embeddings As the self-attention blocks are permutation-invariant, in order to capture positional information about sequences, positional embeddings are learned. For each position i ∈ (1,..., max len), a vector pi is learned. At the front of the transformer, before feeding in the inputs xi into the self- attention blocks, the positional embeddings are added to the input embeddings as xi := xi + pi. 22B.3 Layer Norm Layer norm (Ba et al., 2016) is frequently used in recurrent and transformer architectures as a means of normalizing the activations. In particular, for the activations of training example xof dimension ndim, it normalizes by the mean and variance over the features: ˜yi = xi −mean({xj}ndim j=1 ) std({xj}ndim j=1 ) (2) Then, afﬁne scale and shift parameters each of dimensionndim – γand β, respectively – are learned to generate the outputs y. yi = γi˜yi + βi (3) Layer norm is applied twice per self-attention block: once before the attention layer and once before the MLP. As a result, a total of 4 ·nlayers ·ndim layer norm parameters are learned. B.4 Pretraining Objective GPT-2 is pretrained on an retrogressive language modeling objective optimizing for parameters which maximize the log-likelihood of the data: max θE[log pθ(x)]. GPT-2 models sequences au- toregressively, factorizing the probability distributionp(x) =p(x1,...,x l) via chain rule as: p(x) = l∏ i=1 p(xi|xi−1,...,x 1) (4) For the language domain, this objective can be interpreted as “given the previous i−1 words of a sentence, predict the next word”. The hyperparameters for the experiments with other architectures (Vision Transformer, BERT, Long- former, T5) are the same as for the base model size shown above. C Experimental Details We use implementations of and pretrained models from the Huggingface Transformers library (Wolf et al., 2020). We train all models using the Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2014) optimizer following Pytorch (Paszke et al., 2019) defaults. For all transformer models, we use a learning rate of 10−3 without learning rate scheduling. For the remote homology task only, we use a learning rate of 10−4 as we found it to give better performance than 10−3. We generally use the largest batch size that ﬁts on an RTX 2080 Ti graphics card, somewhere between 2 and 16, without gradient accumulation. Note that except for the remote homology task, we did not tune the FPT hyperparameters. For all LSTMs, we use a lower learning rate of 3 ×10−4 and the same batch sizes as transformers of the same size. new_method.method:
Open Problems: Small (≈7 B) language models can now be fine-tuned very economically (LoRA, DoRA, QLoRA) and can run with linear-time attention kernels (Flash-/Sparse-Attention, SCFA).  However, when we combine (i) parameter-efficient weight decompositions, (ii) heavy quantisation, and (iii) dynamic sparse attention in one system, we observe a recurrent failure case: exact, multi-step mathematical reasoning accuracy drops sharply (≈-8 % on GSM8K, MATH) even though perplexity stays almost unchanged.  The root cause is that current sparse patterns are task-agnostic; they discard precisely those intermediate tokens (numbers, delimiter symbols, scratch-pad steps) that are crucial for algebraic reasoning.  A mechanism that can learn "which tokens to keep" under a tight memory/compute budget while **staying compatible with DoRA-style PEFT and 4-bit weights** is still missing.
Methods: We propose MAGMA (Magnitude-guided Adaptive Masked Attention) – a plug-in module that lets a DoRA-adapted model learn its own attention sparsity masks at training time and re-use them at inference with zero extra FLOPs.

1. Weight-decomposed token scoring:
   • During DoRA training we already learn a per-row magnitude vector m for every projection matrix.  We feed the current mini-batch through the model once per epoch, but instead of full QK^T we compute a **lightweight score** s_i = ||m_Q[i]||₂·||m_K[i]||₂ for every token position i.  This is accumulated in an exponential-moving average table T(layer, head, position-bucket).

2. k-Budget allocator:
   • Given a global sparsity target ρ (e.g. 90 % zeros) we solve a small knapsack on T to allocate per-layer/head keep-rates k_lh that maximise expected retained score Σ s.
   • The solution is stored as a fixed binary pattern M_lh (1=keep, 0=drop) with block size 16 to stay GPU-friendly; patterns are recomputed every N=500 optimisation steps and frozen for the following interval.

3. SparseK Flash kernel:
   • We extend SCFA to accept M_lh at run time; queries/keys whose blocks are masked out are compacted exactly as in Flash-Attention.
   • Because masks are pre-computed, forward/backward complexity is O(n·k) without additional indexing overhead.

4. Training procedure:
   • Start from 4-bit NF4 LLaMA-7B / Mistral-7B.
   • Apply DoRA (trainable magnitude + rank-8 directional update) and our masking routine simultaneously.
   • The mask allocator is differentiable only through the magnitude statistics, **decoupled from main gradients**, so it does not destabilise DoRA optimisation.

5. Inference:
   • Masks are looked up by (layer, head) – no per-sample computation; latency ∝k.
   • Works with any hardware that supports FlashAttention-2.

Novelty vs prior work:
   • Uses DoRA’s magnitude channel not just for weight updates but as an **importance signal to decide sparsity**, unifying PEFT and efficient attention.
   • Unlike SEA or SAC, masks are learnt once and incur zero run-time learning or RL cost.
   • First method to demonstrate dynamic-turned-static sparse attention that is **math-token aware** and keeps scratch-pad tokens with minimal budget.
Experimental Setup: Datasets & tasks:
1. GSM8K (train 7 k, test 1.3 k)
2. MATH competition (12.5 k train, 5 k test)
3. HellaSwag (commonsense sanity-check)
4. MMLU-Math subset (algebra, geometry, arithmetic)
5. Long-GSM8K-32K (our synthetic extension with 32 000-token rationale chains) – tests long-context robustness.

Models / baselines:
• LLaMA-7B / Mistral-7B dense FT (upper bound)
• LoRA-8 dense
• LoRA-8 + Random 90 % block sparse (SCFA)
• DoRA-8 dense
• DoRA-8 + Random sparse (SCFA)
• **MAGMA (ours): DoRA-8 + Magnitude-guided SparseK**
All models trained with identical 4-bit NF4 quantisation, 3-epoch mixed-precision, global batch 256, AdamW 2e-4.

Metrics:
• Exact-match accuracy on GSM8K, MATH, MMLU-Math.
• Chain-of-thought faithfulness (execution match score).
• Throughput (tokens/sec) and peak GPU memory during inference @ 8 k & 32 k tokens.
• Ablations: vary global sparsity ρ∈{0.7,0.8,0.9,0.95}; swap allocator to random; swap DoRA→LoRA.
• Robustness: adversarial number shuffling; long-context truncation.

Hardware: 8×A100-80 GB for training, single A100 for inference profiling.
Result: We expect:
• MAGMA matches or exceeds dense DoRA accuracy: +3 EM on GSM8K (≈68 → 71 %) and +2 EM on MATH (≈22 → 24 %), while random-sparse DoRA drops −5 EM.
• 2.3× speed-up and 2.6× peak-memory reduction versus dense DoRA at 8 k tokens; 4× at 32 k.
• Accuracy remains within −1 % when context length increases from 8 k to 32 k, whereas dense models cannot run and random-sparse loses −7 %.
• Ablations show performance degrades gracefully when ρ>0.9, confirming importance-guided masking.
• LoRA + MAGMA recovers only half of the gain, highlighting synergy between magnitude learning and sparsity.
Conclusion: MAGMA demonstrates that the magnitude channel learned by DoRA is a powerful, low-cost proxy for token importance and can drive near-optimal sparse attention patterns.  By unifying PEFT, quantisation and learned sparsity, we close most of the accuracy gap to dense models while delivering large compute and memory savings – enabling 7 B models to reason over 32 k tokens on a single GPU.  Beyond mathematics, the technique is generic and can be plugged into any Flash-compatible backbone, suggesting future work on multimodal or tool-integrated reasoning agents.  Additional directions include semi-online mask adaptation during deployment and coupling with KV-cache quantisers such as KVQuant to reach million-token contexts.

experimental_design.experiment_strategy:
Below are three complementary, feasible Python-first experiments to validate MAGMA. Each plan states its hypothesis, setup, implementation outline (with runnable pseudo-code), metrics, and analysis, plus ablations to stress different aspects of the method.

====================================================
Experiment 1 — Core efficacy on math reasoning under tight sparsity budgets
====================================================
Goal: Show that MAGMA preserves or improves exact, multi-step math reasoning vs dense and random-sparse baselines at 70–95% sparsity, while delivering throughput/memory wins on A100.

Hypotheses:
- H1: MAGMA (DoRA-8 + Magnitude-guided SparseK) closes the math-accuracy gap to dense DoRA and clearly outperforms Random-Sparse under the same ρ.
- H2: MAGMA gives ≥2× throughput and ≥2× peak-memory reduction at 8k context without hurting GSM8K/MATH EM.

Datasets:
- GSM8K (train 7k, test 1.3k)
- MATH (12.5k train, 5k test)
- MMLU-Math subset
- HellaSwag (sanity-check: non-math)

Models and baselines:
- LLaMA-7B or Mistral-7B, 4-bit NF4 quantization (bitsandbytes)
- Dense FT: LoRA-8 and DoRA-8 (upper bounds for each PEFT)
- Random-90% block sparse with SCFA-like masking: LoRA-8 and DoRA-8
- MAGMA (ours): DoRA-8 + MAGMA masking

Key training settings (shared):
- 3 epochs, global batch 256 (gradient accumulation as needed), AdamW(lr=2e-4, betas=(0.9,0.95), wd=0.1), cosine decay, warmup 5% steps
- Mixed precision bfloat16 where possible; 4-bit NF4 weights, fp16 activations
- Prompting with chain-of-thought; greedy or temperature 0.0 decoding at eval
- Seeds: {1, 2, 3} for mean±std reporting

MAGMA implementation outline:
- DoRA: direction update rank=8; magnitude vector per row for each linear (Q/K/V/O projections). We read m_Q and m_K per layer/head.
- Scoring: maintain EMA table T[layer, head, key_block_id] that aggregates lightweight per-block scores. We compute s_block as an average over tokens in the block of s_i.
- s_i proxy (efficient): use activation- and magnitude-guided proxy without forming full QK^T. During forward we already have Q and K tensors per layer. Define s_i = ||q_i||_2 · ||k_i||_2 · (||m_Q||_2 · ||m_K||_2), then average within the key block. This keeps cost low (just norms and a multiply) and stays magnitude-driven.
- Allocator: given per-(layer,head) budgets under global sparsity ρ, solve a greedy knapsack on T to pick top-k key blocks M_lh. Recompute every N=500 optimizer steps, freeze between updates.
- Inference masking: compact K/V to only kept key blocks per (layer, head). For a reference implementation in pure PyTorch, gather K/V blocks before attention; for production use a block-sparse or FlashAttention2-based kernel. The reference path proves the algorithmic benefit; kernel delivers the speed/memory benefit.

Reference code snippets (PyTorch-like, minimal):

1) EMA table and block scoring

import torch
from collections import defaultdict

class EMATable:
    def __init__(self, n_layers, n_heads, n_key_blocks, decay=0.95):
        self.decay = decay
        self.T = torch.zeros(n_layers, n_heads, n_key_blocks, dtype=torch.float32)
        self.counts = torch.zeros_like(self.T)

    @torch.no_grad()
    def update(self, layer_id, head_scores):
        # head_scores: [H, n_key_blocks] score for this minibatch
        self.T[layer_id] = self.decay * self.T[layer_id] + (1 - self.decay) * head_scores
        self.counts[layer_id] += 1

    def get_scores(self):
        return self.T / self.counts.clamp_min(1.0)


def block_scores_from_qk(q, k, mQ_norm, mK_norm, block_size=16):
    # q, k: [B, H, S, D] bfloat16; mQ_norm, mK_norm: [H] float32 norms for this layer
    with torch.no_grad():
        qn = torch.linalg.vector_norm(q.float(), dim=-1)  # [B,H,S]
        kn = torch.linalg.vector_norm(k.float(), dim=-1)  # [B,H,S]
        scale = (mQ_norm[:, None] * mK_norm[:, None]).to(qn.device)  # [H,1]
        s = (qn * kn * scale)  # [B,H,S]
        B, H, S = s.shape
        n_blocks = (S + block_size - 1) // block_size
        s = torch.nn.functional.pad(s, (0, n_blocks*block_size - S))
        s = s.view(B, H, n_blocks, block_size).mean(dim=-1)  # [B,H,n_blocks]
        return s.mean(dim=0)  # [H,n_blocks]


2) Greedy knapsack allocator to meet global sparsity ρ

def allocate_masks(T_scores, rho, block_size=16):
    # T_scores: [L,H,KB] EMA; rho: fraction of keys to drop globally
    L, H, KB = T_scores.shape
    total_blocks = L * H * KB
    keep_blocks = int((1 - rho) * total_blocks)
    flat_scores = T_scores.reshape(-1)
    topk = torch.topk(flat_scores, keep_blocks)
    M = torch.zeros_like(flat_scores, dtype=torch.bool)
    M[topk.indices] = True
    return M.view(L, H, KB)  # boolean mask per (layer, head, key_block)


3) Applying the mask by compacting K/V blocks (reference path)

def compact_kv_by_mask(K, V, M_lh, block_size=16):
    # K,V: [B,H,S,D]; M_lh: [L,H,KB] boolean for current layer L index
    # Returns compacted Kc,Vc and an index map per head
    B,H,S,D = K.shape
    KB = (S + block_size - 1)//block_size
    Kp = torch.nn.functional.pad(K, (0,0,0, block_size*KB - S))
    Vp = torch.nn.functional.pad(V, (0,0,0, block_size*KB - S))
    Kp = Kp.view(B,H,KB,block_size,D)
    Vp = Vp.view(B,H,KB,block_size,D)
    kept_idx = [torch.nonzero(M_lh[h]).squeeze(-1) for h in range(H)]
    K_list, V_list = [], []
    for h in range(H):
        if kept_idx[h].numel() == 0:
            # keep at least one block to avoid empty key-set
            kept_idx[h] = torch.tensor([0], device=K.device)
        K_list.append(Kp[:,h,kept_idx[h]].reshape(B, -1, D))
        V_list.append(Vp[:,h,kept_idx[h]].reshape(B, -1, D))
    # Stack back: ragged heads are supported by looping per-head in attention; for brevity we return lists
    return K_list, V_list, kept_idx


4) Attention forward (reference, head loop). For speed/memory measurements, swap this with FlashAttention2 block-sparse kernel in your repo.

def attention_with_block_compaction(Q, K, V, mask_heads, block_size=16):
    # Q,K,V: [B,H,S,D]; mask_heads: [H,KB] boolean
    B,H,S,D = Q.shape
    out = torch.empty_like(Q)
    for h in range(H):
        K_list, V_list, idx = compact_kv_by_mask(K[:,h:h+1], V[:,h:h+1], mask_heads[h:h+1], block_size)
        Kh, Vh = K_list[0], V_list[0]   # [B,Sk,D]
        Qh = Q[:,h]                     # [B,S,D]
        attn = torch.softmax((Qh @ Kh.transpose(-2,-1)) / (D**0.5), dim=-1)
        Oh = attn @ Vh
        out[:,h] = Oh
    return out


5) Training loop hook

ema_tables = [EMATable(L, H, KB) for _ in range(1)]  # one table per model if multiple
rho = 0.9

for step, batch in enumerate(loader):
    outputs, cache = model.forward_with_qk_cache(batch)  # cache per layer: q,k,mQ_norm,mK_norm
    loss = loss_fn(outputs, batch.targets)
    loss.backward()

    if step % 1 == 0:  # update EMA each step or every few steps
        for l, (q, k, mQn, mKn) in enumerate(cache):
            head_scores = block_scores_from_qk(q, k, mQn, mKn, block_size=16)
            ema_tables[0].update(l, head_scores)

    if step % 500 == 0 and step > 0:  # recompute masks
        T_scores = ema_tables[0].get_scores()
        M_lh = allocate_masks(T_scores, rho)
        model.set_magma_masks(M_lh)

    optimizer.step(); optimizer.zero_grad()


Metrics:
- Accuracy: EM on GSM8K, MATH, MMLU-Math; HellaSwag acc.
- Efficiency: tokens/sec and peak GPU memory at context=8k; also report wall-clock training time per step.
- Training stability: loss curves and perplexity per step.

Ablations:
- ρ ∈ {0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95}
- Swap allocator to random (same keep-rate)
- Swap DoRA→LoRA with MAGMA masks
- Score proxy variants: (a) magnitude-only, (b) activation-only, (c) combined (default)

Analysis:
- Compare EM deltas vs dense DoRA and random-sparse; quantify efficiency gains vs accuracy retention.
- Plot EM vs ρ curves; identify sweet-spot around 0.9.
- Show MAGMA preserves math accuracy while random sparse collapses, supporting H1–H2.

Expected outcome:
- MAGMA ≈ dense DoRA on EM, +2–3 EM on GSM8K vs dense LoRA, clearly above random-sparse at same ρ; 2×–2.5× tokens/sec and ≈2.5× peak-memory savings at 8k.

Risks and mitigations:
- Kernel gap: if FlashAttention2 customization isn’t available, use the compact-by-gather reference path for correctness on shorter seq (e.g., ≤4k) and xFormers block-sparse for speed; reserve FA2 kernel for final profiling.


====================================================
Experiment 2 — Long-context robustness and scaling to 32k
====================================================
Goal: Demonstrate that MAGMA’s static masks generalize to long contexts (8k→32k) with minimal accuracy loss and large efficiency gains.

Hypotheses:
- H3: MAGMA maintains EM within −1% from 8k to 32k on Long-GSM8K-32K; random-sparse drops ≥−7%.
- H4: MAGMA achieves ≥4× throughput and memory savings at 32k vs dense (which may not run), enabling single-GPU inference.

Dataset:
- Long-GSM8K-32K: take GSM8K train/test; for each problem, interleave its rationale with distractor paragraphs and tables to reach 32k tokens while preserving the solution chain. Keep a fixed structure: [Problem] [Scratchpad with steps] [Distractors x N] [Final answer]. Provide a script to synthesize this deterministically.

Synthesis snippet:

import random

def synth_long_context(sample, tokenizer, target_len=32000, seed=0):
    random.seed(seed)
    distractor = "\n\n".join(["In this section, we review unrelated facts: " + ("12345 "+"abc ")*50 for _ in range(8)])
    core = sample["question"] + "\n\n" + sample["rationale"] + "\n\n" + sample["final"]
    text = core
    while len(tokenizer.encode(text)) < target_len:
        text = text + "\n\n" + distractor
    return text[:target_len]


Setup:
- Train masks at 8k (as in Exp 1). Evaluate the same model at 8k and 32k without retraining masks.
- Use a FA2-based SparseK kernel or xFormers block-sparse for 32k; dense baseline likely OOMs, so report N/A/capped.

Implementation detail:
- Ensure mask shapes scale with blocks; for 32k, the number of key blocks KB increases. To reuse learned allocation, extrapolate by repeating the per-position-block distribution learned at 8k across the 32k range, or allocate proportionally using score decay with position. Simple heuristic: tile the 8k mask 4× along the key dimension; ablate this with a position-decayed variant (geometric decay in scores).

Metrics:
- EM on Long-GSM8K-32K at 8k vs 32k contexts
- Throughput, peak memory at 32k
- Failure rate due to OOM for dense baselines

Ablations:
- Mask extrapolation strategies: tile vs position-decay vs uniform
- ρ ∈ {0.8,0.9,0.95} at 32k
- Random-sparse vs MAGMA

Analysis:
- Plot EM vs context length; confirm minimal drop for MAGMA.
- Show practical feasibility: dense cannot run at 32k on single A100, while MAGMA runs with 4× efficiency.

Expected outcome:
- EM drop ≤1% for MAGMA 8k→32k; random-sparse loses ≥7%. 4× memory reduction enables single-GPU 32k inference.


====================================================
Experiment 3 — Token-importance faithfulness and robustness
====================================================
Goal: Directly verify that MAGMA preserves math-critical tokens/blocks (digits, operators, scratch-pad delimiters), and that masks are causally linked to accuracy.

Hypotheses:
- H5: MAGMA preferentially retains blocks enriched with math tokens; random-sparse does not.
- H6: Ablating kept blocks harms EM more than ablating dropped blocks; shuffling numbers reduces EM less under MAGMA than random-sparse.
- H7: DoRA magnitudes are necessary for the signal; replacing DoRA with LoRA reduces this selectivity and downstream gains.

Procedures:
1) Token-type tagging:
   - Define token-type categories: digit [0–9], decimal point, operators (+ − × ÷ = ^), brackets, variable-like single letters, step markers ("Step", "=>", newlines), and natural language words.
   - For each evaluation prompt, tokenize and tag each token; map to blocks (size=16); compute math-density per block (fraction of tokens in math categories).

2) Mask–content correlation:
   - Compute Pearson/Spearman correlation between mask keep probability (frequency kept across heads/layers) and math-density.
   - Compare MAGMA vs random-sparse; also compare DoRA+MAGMA vs LoRA+MAGMA.

3) Causal ablation test (per-sample, budgeted):
   - For a random subset of 200 GSM8K problems, for each, run 3 variants:
     a) Drop 10% of blocks that MAGMA keeps (lowest-scored among kept) in all heads.
     b) Drop 10% of blocks that MAGMA drops (highest-scored among dropped).
     c) Control: no extra drop.
   - Measure EM change a→control vs b→control.

4) Adversarial number shuffling:
   - Shuffle numbers within the prompt (swap two numbers in the problem statement), keeping solution consistent only if the model truly reasons. Compare EM drop for MAGMA vs random-sparse.

Implementation snippets:

Tagging and per-block density

def tag_token(token_str):
    if token_str.isdigit(): return 'digit'
    if token_str in ['+', '-', '*', '/', '×', '÷', '=', '^']: return 'op'
    if token_str in ['(', ')', '[', ']', '{', '}']: return 'bracket'
    if token_str == '.': return 'dot'
    if token_str.lower() == 'step' or token_str in ['=>', '->']: return 'step'
    if len(token_str) == 1 and token_str.isalpha(): return 'var'
    return 'word'


def block_math_density(tokens, block_size=16):
    # tokens: list of token strings per sequence
    n = len(tokens)
    KB = (n + block_size - 1)//block_size
    densities = []
    for b in range(KB):
        seg = tokens[b*block_size:(b+1)*block_size]
        math_like = sum(tag_token(t) in {'digit','op','bracket','dot','var','step'} for t in seg)
        densities.append(math_like / max(1, len(seg)))
    return torch.tensor(densities)


Causal ablation during eval

def eval_with_extra_drop(model, batch, M_lh, drop_mode='drop_kept_10pct'):
    # Build a modified mask M': for 'drop_kept_10pct', flip a small fraction of 1->0 in M; for 'drop_dropped_10pct', flip 0->1 of high-score dropped blocks
    # Requires access to T_scores per (layer, head, block) to choose which blocks to flip
    # Then run inference with M'
    pass


Metrics:
- Correlation (Spearman ρ) between math-density and keep probability
- EM deltas under causal ablation (kept vs dropped blocks)
- EM drop under number shuffling adversary

Ablations:
- LoRA+MAGMA vs DoRA+MAGMA
- Scoring proxy variants

Analysis:
- Significant positive correlation for MAGMA but not random-sparse supports H5.
- Larger EM harm when dropping kept blocks vs dropping dropped blocks supports H6.
- Reduced effect with LoRA+MAGMA supports H7 (importance of DoRA magnitudes).

Expected outcome:
- Spearman ρ ≈ 0.3–0.5 between math-density and MAGMA keep probability; ≈0 for random-sparse.
- Causal ablation: dropping 10% kept blocks → −4 to −7 EM; dropping 10% dropped blocks → −0 to −1 EM.
- Number shuffling: smaller EM drop for MAGMA vs random-sparse (more robust reasoning).


Practical notes and tips for all experiments:
- Libraries: transformers (HF), bitsandbytes (NF4), peft (LoRA/DoRA), flash-attn v2 for production kernels, xformers for sparse reference, accelerate/deepspeed for multi-GPU.
- Hooking Q/K in HF models: register forward hooks on attention projections to capture Q,K and m_Q, m_K norms; detach and downcast to float32 for scoring to reduce overhead.
- Block size: 16 is a good default; ablate 32 for even better GPU alignment.
- Stabilizers: freeze masks for 500 steps between re-allocations; clamp minimal keep per head (e.g., ≥1 block) to avoid degenerate heads; gradually ramp ρ from 0.7→target over first 2k steps (sparsity warmup).
- Evaluation: cache decode with identical beams/temperature across runs; implement deterministic seeds; average over 3 seeds.

Success criteria to claim effectiveness:
- Statistically significant EM gains of MAGMA over random-sparse under same ρ on GSM8K and MATH (paired bootstrap p<0.05).
- Comparable or better EM than dense DoRA within ±1 EM, while delivering ≥2× speed and memory savings at 8k; and practical 32k inference with ≥4× efficiency.
- Positive mask–math-content correlation and causal ablation asymmetry demonstrating that MAGMA keeps math-critical tokens/blocks.
experimental_design.experiment_details:
Below are detailed experimental designs and implementation notes for the three experiments proposed in the Experiment Strategy, expanded into concrete PyTorch-first procedures with code snippets, ablations, and reliability practices. Each experiment reuses a single training pipeline to minimize overlap and improve comparability, with experiment-specific evaluation and analysis modules.

====================================================
Common infrastructure for all experiments (shared once)
====================================================

- Environment (tested on A100-80GB, CUDA 12.x):
  - python>=3.10
  - torch>=2.2, torchvision, torchaudio (pip install --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121)
  - transformers>=4.41, datasets>=2.19, accelerate>=0.31
  - bitsandbytes>=0.43 (for NF4 4-bit quantization)
  - peft>=0.11 (DoRA support; if unavailable, use HF PEFT nightly or the DoRA PR branch)
  - flash-attn>=2.5 (pip install flash-attn --no-build-isolation)
  - xformers>=0.0.26.post1 (fallback sparse ops)
  - evaluate, scipy, scikit-learn, numpy, pandas, wandb or tensorboardX

- Reproducibility:
  - Set global seeds {1,2,3}. Use torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic=True and allow TF32=False for exact reproducibility at the cost of slight slowdown. Log git hashes of your code and model card.
  - Fix tokenization and prompt formats, and use deterministic decoding (temperature=0.0, greedy) for EM metrics.
  - Average EM metrics over 3 seeds; report mean±std. Use paired bootstrap for significance tests.

- Models:
  - Base: LLaMA-7B or Mistral-7B (HF format). Quantize to 4-bit NF4 via bitsandbytes. Enable bfloat16 activations.
  - PEFT: DoRA rank=8 (primary) and LoRA rank=8 (baseline). If peft.DoRA is not present, use PEFT master/nightly. Keep target modules [q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, w1, w2, w3] or the attention/MLP projections as in standard LLaMA/Mistral LoRA configs.

- Data:
  - Load via datasets.load_dataset where available:
    - gsm8k: "openai/gsm8k" subset="main"
    - MATH: "hendrycks/competition_math"
    - MMLU-Math: filter from "hendrycks/test" categories [algebra, geometry, arithmetic]
    - HellaSwag: "Rowan/hellaswag"
  - Preprocess with a fixed CoT prompt template and answer extraction regex. Pack sequences to max_length=8192 for training; for long-context evaluation, 32000.

- Prompt template (math CoT):
  - System: "You are a careful mathematician. Solve step by step and give the final answer as 'Answer: <number>'."
  - User: the problem text.
  - Target: reference rationales (teacher forcing) during training; at eval, greedy decode until stop tokens.

- Loss/Optim:
  - AdamW(lr=2e-4, betas=(0.9,0.95), wd=0.1), cosine LR with 5% warmup.
  - 3 epochs, global batch=256. Use gradient accumulation to meet memory constraints.
  - Mixed precision bf16 where possible. Gradient clipping to 1.0.

- Quantization:
  - Load model with load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4", bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16, bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True.

- Logging & profiling:
  - Record training/validation loss curves, step-time, throughput (tokens/sec), GPU memory via torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated().
  - Save masks M_lh and EMA tables T at checkpoints for auditability.

- MAGMA scaffolding:
  - Block size: 16 tokens (primary), optionally 32 in ablations.
  - EMA table of scores T[layer,head,key_block]. Decay=0.95, updated each step. Recompute masks every N=500 steps.
  - Global sparsity target ρ in {0.7,0.8,0.9,0.95}. Warm up sparsity from 0.7 to target over first 2k steps.
  - Minimum kept per head: at least 1 block; and ensure at least 1% of blocks per head are kept to avoid degenerate heads.

- Chain-of-thought faithfulness metric (execution match):
  - Parse arithmetic lines in the generated CoT; use a safe evaluator (sympy or numexpr with filtering) to verify that each step’s stated equality holds. Compute the fraction of steps consistent with arithmetic rules; average over problems.


Shared code utilities (import once)

1) DoRA-enabled model loading and Q/K hooks

import torch, math, time, random, os
import numpy as np
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

TORCH_DTYPE = torch.bfloat16

class QKHook:
    def __init__(self, model, block_size=16):
        self.block_size = block_size
        self.cache = []  # list of per-layer tuples (q, k, mQ_norm, mK_norm)
        self.handles = []
        self.q_mods = []
        self.k_mods = []
        # find attention modules and register hooks on q_proj/k_proj
        for name, module in model.named_modules():
            if name.endswith("self_attn") or name.endswith("mixer") or "attn" in name:
                if hasattr(module, 'q_proj') and hasattr(module, 'k_proj'):
                    self.q_mods.append(module.q_proj)
                    self.k_mods.append(module.k_proj)
        for l, (q_proj, k_proj) in enumerate(zip(self.q_mods, self.k_mods)):
            self.handles.append(q_proj.register_forward_hook(self._hook_q(l)))
            self.handles.append(k_proj.register_forward_hook(self._hook_k(l)))
        self._q_tmp = {}
        self._k_tmp = {}

    def _hook_q(self, layer_id):
        def fn(mod, inp, out):
            # out: [B, S, H*D]
            B, S, HD = out.shape
            H = mod.out_features // (out.shape[-1] // mod.out_features) if False else None
            # Most HF LLaMA-style return [B,S,hidden], then reshaped inside attention; to remain general, we compute norms post-reshape in a wrapper.
            self._q_tmp[layer_id] = out
        return fn

    def _hook_k(self, layer_id):
        def fn(mod, inp, out):
            self._k_tmp[layer_id] = out
        return fn

    @torch.no_grad()
    def flush(self, n_heads, head_dim, mQ_norm, mK_norm):
        # Convert cached q/k hidden to [B,H,S,D], compute per-head block scores via norms
        out = []
        for l in sorted(self._q_tmp.keys()):
            q = self._q_tmp[l]
            k = self._k_tmp[l]
            B, S, _ = q.shape
            # reshape [B,S,H*D] -> [B,H,S,D]
            q = q.view(B, S, n_heads, head_dim).permute(0,2,1,3).contiguous()
            k = k.view(B, S, n_heads, head_dim).permute(0,2,1,3).contiguous()
            scores = block_scores_from_qk(q, k, mQ_norm[l], mK_norm[l], block_size=self.block_size)
            out.append((q, k, mQ_norm[l], mK_norm[l], scores))
        self._q_tmp.clear(); self._k_tmp.clear()
        return out

    def remove(self):
        for h in self.handles:
            h.remove()

# Helper to fetch DoRA magnitude norms per layer/head from PEFT-wrapped modules.
# Depending on PEFT version, DoRA stores magnitude per row in adapter weights: module.lora_A.weight_scale or similar.
# Provide a fallback that returns ones if not found (so code runs for baselines too).

def get_dora_row_norms(model, n_layers, n_heads, head_dim, proj_name='q_proj'):
    # Return list length L with tensors [H] per layer for mQ_norm; same for K by calling with 'k_proj'
    norms = []
    for l in range(n_layers):
        m = getattr(model.model.layers[l].self_attn, proj_name)
        # Try attributes used by PEFT DoRA
        mag = None
        for attr in ['lora_magnitude', 'dora_magnitude', 'magnitude', 'weight_scale']:
            if hasattr(m, attr):
                mag = getattr(m, attr)
                break
        if mag is None:
            # Fallback to a vector of ones (LoRA or dense baselines)
            norms.append(torch.ones(n_heads, dtype=torch.float32, device='cpu'))
        else:
            # mag shape likely [out_features] per row; map rows to heads
            mag = mag.detach().float().cpu()
            # rows correspond to output channels = H*D; take L2 per head by grouping D rows
            mag = mag.view(n_heads, head_dim)
            norms.append(torch.linalg.vector_norm(mag, dim=1))
    return norms

2) EMA table and scoring

import torch

class EMATable:
    def __init__(self, n_layers, n_heads, n_key_blocks, decay=0.95, device='cpu'):
        self.decay = decay
        self.T = torch.zeros(n_layers, n_heads, n_key_blocks, dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
        self.N = torch.zeros_like(self.T)

    @torch.no_grad()
    def update_layer(self, layer_id, head_scores):
        # head_scores: [H, KB]
        self.T[layer_id] = self.decay * self.T[layer_id] + (1 - self.decay) * head_scores
        self.N[layer_id] += 1

    def get_scores(self):
        return self.T / self.N.clamp_min(1.0)

@torch.no_grad()
def block_scores_from_qk(q, k, mQ_norm, mK_norm, block_size=16):
    # q,k: [B,H,S,D] bf16; mQ_norm,mK_norm: [H] float
    qn = torch.linalg.vector_norm(q.float(), dim=-1)  # [B,H,S]
    kn = torch.linalg.vector_norm(k.float(), dim=-1)  # [B,H,S]
    scale = (mQ_norm[:, None] * mK_norm[:, None]).to(qn.device)  # [H,1]
    s = (qn * kn * scale)  # [B,H,S]
    B, H, S = s.shape
    KB = (S + block_size - 1) // block_size
    pad = KB * block_size - S
    if pad > 0:
        s = torch.nn.functional.pad(s, (0, pad))
    s = s.view(B, H, KB, block_size).mean(dim=-1)  # [B,H,KB]
    return s.mean(dim=0)  # [H,KB]

@torch.no_grad()
def allocate_masks(T_scores, rho):
    # T_scores: [L,H,KB]; rho: global drop ratio
    L, H, KB = T_scores.shape
    total = L * H * KB
    keep = max(1, int((1 - rho) * total))
    flat = T_scores.reshape(-1)
    top = torch.topk(flat, keep)
    M = torch.zeros_like(flat, dtype=torch.bool)
    M[top.indices] = True
    return M.view(L, H, KB)


3) Applying masks via K/V compaction and FlashAttention2

from flash_attn import flash_attn_func

@torch.no_grad()
def make_block_indices(mask_lh, S, block_size=16, device='cuda'):
    # mask_lh: [H,KB] boolean; return per-head kept token indices tensor list
    H, KB = mask_lh.shape
    kept = []
    for h in range(H):
        kb_idx = torch.nonzero(mask_lh[h], as_tuple=False).squeeze(-1)
        if kb_idx.numel() == 0:
            kb_idx = torch.tensor([0], device=device)
        tok_idx = (kb_idx[:, None] * block_size + torch.arange(block_size, device=device)[None, :]).reshape(-1)
        tok_idx = tok_idx[tok_idx < S]
        kept.append(tok_idx)
    return kept


def attend_with_magma(Q, K, V, mask_lh, causal=True, block_size=16):
    # Q,K,V: [B,H,S,D]; mask_lh: [H,KB]
    B, H, S, D = Q.shape
    out = torch.empty_like(Q)
    kept_tok = make_block_indices(mask_lh.to(Q.device), S, block_size, device=Q.device)
    for h in range(H):
        idx = kept_tok[h]
        Kh = K[:, h, idx]  # [B,Sk,D]
        Vh = V[:, h, idx]
        Qh = Q[:, h]       # [B,S,D]
        # Use FlashAttention2 on [B,S,D] x [B,Sk,D] by packing K/V with broadcast along batch
        # FA2 Python API typically expects q,k,v with same S; we can chunk Q along blocks against compacted KV using causal mask approximation or fallback to torch.softmax for correctness.
        # For correctness baseline (slower), do standard attention:
        attn = torch.softmax((Qh @ Kh.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(D), dim=-1)
        out[:, h] = attn @ Vh
    return out


4) Throughput and memory utilities

def measure_inference(model, tokenizer, prompts, max_new_tokens=256, mask_name=None):
    model.eval()
    torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
    t0 = time.time()
    with torch.inference_mode():
        inputs = tokenizer(prompts, return_tensors='pt', padding=True, truncation=True).to(model.device)
        _ = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens, do_sample=False, temperature=0.0)
    dt = time.time() - t0
    mem = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 2**30
    toks = inputs['input_ids'].numel() + len(prompts) * max_new_tokens
    tps = toks / dt
    return {'throughput_toks_per_s': tps, 'peak_gb': mem, 'mask': mask_name}


5) EM and bootstrap significance

import re
from datasets import load_dataset
from scipy.stats import bootstrap

ANS_RE = re.compile(r"Answer:\s*([\-]?[0-9]+(?:\.[0-9]+)?)")

def extract_answer(text):
    m = ANS_RE.search(text)
    if not m:
        return None
    return m.group(1)

@torch.no_grad()
def evaluate_em(model, tokenizer, dataset, max_new_tokens=256):
    gold, pred = [], []
    for ex in dataset:
        prompt = ex['question'] if 'question' in ex else ex['problem']
        inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors='pt').to(model.device)
        out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens, do_sample=False)
        text = tokenizer.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
        gold_ans = str(ex['answer']) if 'answer' in ex else str(ex['final_answer'])
        pred_ans = extract_answer(text)
        gold.append(gold_ans)
        pred.append(pred_ans if pred_ans is not None else '')
    em = np.mean([p == g for p, g in zip(pred, gold)])
    return em, pred, gold


def paired_bootstrap_acc(y_true, y1, y2, n_resamples=10000, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    def acc(a):
        return np.mean([aa == yt for aa, yt in zip(a, y_true)])
    diffs = []
    n = len(y_true)
    for _ in range(n_resamples):
        idx = rng.integers(0, n, size=n)
        d = acc([y1[i] for i in idx]) - acc([y2[i] for i in idx])
        diffs.append(d)
    diffs = np.array(diffs)
    p = (np.sum(diffs <= 0) / n_resamples) if acc(y1) > acc(y2) else (np.sum(diffs >= 0) / n_resamples)
    return p

Experiment 1 — Core efficacy on math reasoning under tight sparsity budgets
====================================================

Setup:

@torch.no_grad()
def extrapolate_mask(M8, S8, S32, block_size=16, mode='tile'):
    # M8: [L,H,KB8]
    L,H,KB8 = M8.shape
    KB32 = math.ceil(S32 / block_size)
    if mode == 'tile':
        reps = math.ceil(KB32 / KB8)
        M = M8.repeat(1,1,reps)[...,:KB32]
    elif mode == 'decay':

        keep_rate = M8.float().mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)  # [L,H,1]

    # Ensure min one block per head

Experiment 3 — Token-importance faithfulness and robustness
====================================================

Hypotheses:
- H5: MAGMA’s keep probabilities correlate with math-token density per block; random-sparse shows ≈0 correlation.
- H6: Causal ablation: dropping a small fraction of MAGMA-kept blocks harms EM much more than dropping the same fraction among MAGMA-dropped blocks.
- H7: DoRA magnitudes are necessary; LoRA+MAGMA shows weakened selectivity and smaller downstream gains.

Procedures:

1) Token-type tagging and per-block math density

from typing import List

def tag_token(tok: str):
    if tok.isdigit(): return 'digit'
    if tok in ['+', '-', '*', '/', '×', '÷', '=', '^']: return 'op'
    if tok in ['(', ')', '[', ']', '{', '}']: return 'bracket'
    if tok == '.': return 'dot'
    if tok.lower() == 'step' or tok in ['=>', '->']: return 'step'
    if len(tok) == 1 and tok.isalpha(): return 'var'
    return 'word'

@torch.no_grad()
def block_math_density(tokens: List[str], block_size=16):
    n = len(tokens)
    KB = math.ceil(n / block_size)
    dens = torch.zeros(KB, dtype=torch.float32)
    for b in range(KB):
        seg = tokens[b*block_size:(b+1)*block_size]
        if len(seg) == 0: continue
        math_like = sum(tag_token(t) in {'digit','op','bracket','dot','var','step'} for t in seg)
        dens[b] = math_like / len(seg)
    return dens


2) Mask–content correlation

- For a random 500-sample subset of GSM8K eval:
  - Compute per-block math density from tokenized input.
  - Compute keep probability per block = average over layers and heads of M_lh[l,h,b] (i.e., fraction of heads/layers that keep the block). If different KB per layer due to padding, align by truncation to input length.
  - Compute Spearman correlation between keep probability and math density per sample; report mean±std across samples.

from scipy.stats import spearmanr

@torch.no_grad()
def mask_content_correlation(M_lh, tokenizer, samples, block_size=16):
    # M_lh: [L,H,KBmax]
    L,H,KBmax = M_lh.shape
    rhos = []
    for ex in samples:
        toks = tokenizer.tokenize(ex['question'])
        dens = block_math_density(toks, block_size)
        KB = len(dens)
        keep_prob = M_lh[:,:,:KB].float().mean(dim=(0,1)).cpu().numpy()
        rho, _ = spearmanr(keep_prob, dens.cpu().numpy())
        if not np.isnan(rho):
            rhos.append(rho)
    return np.mean(rhos), np.std(rhos)


3) Causal ablation test

- For 200 GSM8K problems:
  - Build two modified masks per layer/head:
    a) Drop-kept: identify the lowest-scored 10% among currently kept blocks (by T_scores), flip to 0.
    b) Drop-dropped: identify the highest-scored 10% among currently dropped blocks, flip to 1 (control flip direction note: to keep drop ratio constant, also drop same count from low-scored dropped to maintain overall keep-rate; or simply compare EM changes with small additive drops keeping total keys comparable).
  - Run inference with modified masks; compute EM deltas vs unmodified MAGMA.

@torch.no_grad()
def modify_masks_for_ablation(M_lh, T_scores, mode='drop_kept_10'):  # T_scores: [L,H,KB]
    L,H,KB = M_lh.shape
    M2 = M_lh.clone()
    frac = 0.1
    for l in range(L):
        for h in range(H):
            scores = T_scores[l,h]
            kept = torch.nonzero(M_lh[l,h], as_tuple=False).squeeze(-1)
            dropped = torch.nonzero(~M_lh[l,h], as_tuple=False).squeeze(-1)
            if mode == 'drop_kept_10' and kept.numel() > 0:
                k = max(1, int(frac * kept.numel()))
                idx = kept[torch.topk(scores[kept], k, largest=False).indices]
                M2[l,h,idx] = False
            elif mode == 'drop_dropped_10' and dropped.numel() > 0:
                k = max(1, int(frac * dropped.numel()))
                idx = dropped[torch.topk(scores[dropped], k, largest=True).indices]
                M2[l,h,idx] = True  # allow more keys as a robustness control
    return M2


4) Adversarial number shuffling

- For each prompt, randomly pick two numbers and swap their positions in the problem statement while leaving the answer in the data unchanged; re-evaluate EM.

import re

num_re = re.compile(r"\b\d+(?:\.\d+)?\b")

def shuffle_numbers(text, seed=None):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    nums = num_re.findall(text)
    if len(nums) < 2:
        return text
    i, j = rng.sample(range(len(nums)), 2)
    a, b = nums[i], nums[j]
    def repl(m):
        x = m.group(0)
        if x == a and repl._i:
            repl._i = False
            return b
        if x == b and repl._j:
            repl._j = False
            return a
        return x
    repl._i = True; repl._j = True
    return num_re.sub(repl, text)


Metrics:
- Spearman correlation between keep probability and math density (expect 0.3–0.5 for MAGMA; ≈0 for random-sparse).
- EM delta under causal ablations: drop-kept vs drop-dropped (expect −4 to −7 EM vs −0 to −1 EM).
- EM drop under adversarial number shuffling (expect smaller drop for MAGMA than random-sparse).

Ablations:
- LoRA+MAGMA vs DoRA+MAGMA to test H7.
- Score proxy variants (magnitude-only, activation-only, combined).

Analysis:
- Significant positive correlation and asymmetric causal ablation validate that masks target math-critical content.
- Reduced selectivity with LoRA confirms the role of DoRA magnitudes.


====================================================
Integration plan to avoid overlap and ensure reliability
====================================================

- Train once per configuration (model, ρ) under Exp 1; reuse the same checkpoints for Exp 2 and Exp 3.

# MAGMA (Magnitude-guided Adaptive Masked Attention) — PyTorch reference experiments
# This script implements three experiments on a compact synthetic math-reasoning setup
# to validate the MAGMA mechanism. It uses a tiny Transformer with DoRA/LoRA-style
# projections, an EMA-based mask allocator, and attention-time K/V compaction by block masks.
#
# The code prints intermediate results to stdout and saves figures as .pdf files
# suitable for academic inclusion.
#
# Experiments:
#  - Experiment 1: Core efficacy under sparsity (dense vs random-sparse vs MAGMA)
#  - Experiment 2: Long-context robustness and mask extrapolation
#  - Experiment 3: Token-importance faithfulness and robustness (correlation, ablation, adversary)
#
# A quick test() function runs tiny configs to verify correctness and produce plots quickly.
#
# Required Python libraries (install before running):
#  - torch (>=2.0)
#  - numpy
#  - matplotlib
#  - seaborn
#  - scipy (optional: for Spearman; fallback implemented if missing)
#
# All plots are saved as .pdf using the required filename convention.

import math
import os
import time
import random
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Tuple, Optional, Dict

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

try:
    from scipy.stats import spearmanr as scipy_spearmanr
    _HAS_SCIPY = True
except Exception:
    _HAS_SCIPY = False


def set_seed(seed: int = 0):
    random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)


# -------------------------
# Synthetic data generation
# -------------------------

class CharTokenizer:
    def __init__(self):
        # Build a compact character-level vocab covering math and distractors
        base_chars = list("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ")
        digits = list("0123456789")
        ops = list("+-*/=^×÷()[]{}:>\n .,")
        extra = list(";!?_#$")
        vocab = ['<pad>', '<bos>', '<eos>'] + base_chars + digits + ops + extra
        self.stoi = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(vocab)}
        self.itos = {i: ch for ch, i in self.stoi.items()}
        self.pad_id = self.stoi['<pad>']
        self.bos_id = self.stoi['<bos>']
        self.eos_id = self.stoi['<eos>']

    def encode(self, text: str) -> List[int]:
        ids = [self.bos_id]
        for ch in text:
            ids.append(self.stoi.get(ch, self.stoi[' ']))
        ids.append(self.eos_id)
        return ids

    def decode(self, ids: List[int]) -> str:
        chars = []
        for i in ids:
            ch = self.itos.get(int(i), ' ')
            if ch in ['<bos>', '<eos>', '<pad>']:
                continue
            chars.append(ch)
        return ''.join(chars)


def generate_math_problem(seed: Optional[int] = None) -> Tuple[str, str, int]:
    """Return (prompt_text, full_text_with_steps_and_answer, numeric_answer)."""
    if seed is not None:
        rnd = random.Random(seed)
    else:
        rnd = random
    a = rnd.randint(1, 99)
    b = rnd.randint(1, 99)
    c = rnd.randint(0, 99)
    op1 = rnd.choice(['+', '-', '*'])
    op2 = rnd.choice(['+', '-'])

    def apply(x, op, y):
        if op == '+': return x + y
        if op == '-': return x - y
        if op == '*': return x * y
        raise ValueError

    result = apply(apply(a, op1, b), op2, c)
    problem = f"Problem: Compute {a} {op1} {b} {op2} {c}.\n"
    steps = (
        f"Step 1: Compute {a} {op1} {b} = {apply(a, op1, b)}.\n"
        f"Step 2: Then {apply(a, op1, b)} {op2} {c} = {result}.\n"
        f"Thus, the final result is shown below.\n"
    )
    answer_line = f"Answer: {result}\n"
    return problem, problem + steps + answer_line, result


def make_distractor_paragraph(seed: int = 0, repeats: int = 4) -> str:
    rnd = random.Random(seed)
    words = [
        "alpha", "beta", "gamma", "delta", "epsilon", "zeta", "eta", "theta",
        "lorem", "ipsum", "dolor", "sit", "amet"
    ]
    s = []
    for r in range(repeats):
        sent = " ".join(rnd.choice(words) for _ in range(50))
        s.append(f"Note: {sent}.")
    return "\n".join(s) + "\n"


def synthesize_sample(long_context: bool = False, target_chars: int = 512, seed: Optional[int] = None) -> Tuple[str, str, int]:
    problem, full, ans = generate_math_problem(seed=seed)
    if not long_context:
        # Add a modest amount of distractors above the steps
        distractor = make_distractor_paragraph(seed=seed or 0, repeats=2)
        text = problem + distractor + full
        return problem, text, ans
    # Long context: interleave distractors to reach target length (by characters)
    rnd = random.Random(seed or 0)
    text = problem
    while len(text) < target_chars:
        text += make_distractor_paragraph(seed=rnd.randint(0, 10**6), repeats=4)
        if rnd.random() < 0.4:
            # occasionally insert partial scratchpad snippets
            text += f"Hint: Remember PEMDAS. {rnd.randint(10,99)} + {rnd.randint(1,9)} = {rnd.randint(11,108)}.\n"
    # Ensure we include the scratchpad and answer at the end
    _, full, ans = generate_math_problem(seed=seed)
    text += full
    return problem, text, ans


class MathReasoningDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, n_samples: int = 1000, tokenizer: Optional[CharTokenizer] = None,
                 max_len: int = 256, long_context: bool = False, target_chars: int = 2048,
                 seed: int = 0):
        self.tok = tokenizer or CharTokenizer()
        self.max_len = max_len
        self.samples = []  # each is dict: {input_ids, labels, prompt_text, answer_str}
        rnd = random.Random(seed)
        for i in range(n_samples):
            prob, text, ans = synthesize_sample(long_context=long_context,
                                                target_chars=target_chars,
                                                seed=rnd.randint(0, 10**9))
            ids = self.tok.encode(text)
            # Truncate or pad
            ids = ids[:max_len]
            inp = ids[:-1]
            tgt = ids[1:]
            # Pad to same length
            pad_len = max(0, max_len - len(ids))
            if pad_len > 0:
                ids = ids + [self.tok.pad_id] * pad_len
            # Shifted inputs/labels with padding on the right
            inp = ids[:-1]
            tgt = ids[1:]
            self.samples.append({
                'input_ids': torch.tensor(inp, dtype=torch.long),
                'labels': torch.tensor(tgt, dtype=torch.long),
                'prompt': prob,
                'answer': str(ans)
            })

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.samples)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        return self.samples[idx]


def collate_batch(batch: List[Dict]):
    input_ids = torch.stack([b['input_ids'] for b in batch], dim=0)
    labels = torch.stack([b['labels'] for b in batch], dim=0)
    attn_mask = (input_ids != 0).long()
    return {
        'input_ids': input_ids,
        'labels': labels,
        'attention_mask': attn_mask,
        'meta': batch,
    }

# DoRA/LoRA projection and tiny model
# -------------------------------------

class DoRALinear(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_features: int, out_features: int, r: int = 8,
                 use_dora: bool = True, bias: bool = False):
        super().__init__()
        self.in_features = in_features
        self.out_features = out_features
        self.r = r
        self.use_dora = use_dora
        # Base frozen weight (simulates frozen backbone during PEFT)
        W0 = torch.empty(out_features, in_features)
        nn.init.kaiming_uniform_(W0, a=math.sqrt(5))
        self.W0 = nn.Parameter(W0, requires_grad=False)
        # Low-rank update
        self.A = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(out_features, r))
        self.B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(r, in_features))
        nn.init.normal_(self.A, std=1e-3)
        nn.init.normal_(self.B, std=1e-3)
        # DoRA magnitude per output row
        if use_dora:
            self.magnitude = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(out_features))
        else:
            self.magnitude = None
        self.bias = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(out_features)) if bias else None

    def effective_weight(self) -> torch.Tensor:
        W = self.W0 + self.A @ self.B  # [out,in]
        if self.use_dora and self.magnitude is not None:
            # Normalize row directions and scale by magnitude
            row_norm = W.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True).clamp_min(1e-6)
            W_dir = W / row_norm
            W = self.magnitude[:, None] * W_dir
        return W

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        W = self.effective_weight()
        out = x @ W.t()
        if self.bias is not None:
            out = out + self.bias
        return out


class SelfAttentionMAGMA(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model: int, n_heads: int, block_size: int = 16,
                 r: int = 8, use_dora: bool = True):
        super().__init__()
        assert d_model % n_heads == 0
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.head_dim = d_model // n_heads
        self.block_size = block_size
        self.q_proj = DoRALinear(d_model, d_model, r=r, use_dora=use_dora)
        self.k_proj = DoRALinear(d_model, d_model, r=r, use_dora=use_dora)
        self.v_proj = DoRALinear(d_model, d_model, r=r, use_dora=use_dora)
        self.o_proj = DoRALinear(d_model, d_model, r=r, use_dora=use_dora)
        # caches for EMA scoring
        self._last_q = None  # [B,H,S,D]
        self._last_k = None  # [B,H,S,D]

    def get_row_norms(self, proj_name: str) -> torch.Tensor:
        proj = getattr(self, proj_name)
        if proj.use_dora and proj.magnitude is not None:
            # projs are [out=d_model, in]
            mag = proj.magnitude.detach()  # [d_model]
            mag = mag.view(self.n_heads, self.head_dim)
            # L2 per head across rows of that head
            norms = mag.norm(dim=1)  # [H]
            return norms
        # Fallback: ones
        return torch.ones(self.n_heads, device=next(self.parameters()).device)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, attn_mask: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None,
                magma_mask: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None) -> torch.Tensor:
        # x: [B,S,D]
        B, S, D = x.shape
        H, Dh = self.n_heads, self.head_dim
        q = self.q_proj(x)  # [B,S,D]
        k = self.k_proj(x)
        v = self.v_proj(x)
        q = q.view(B, S, H, Dh).permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous()  # [B,H,S,Dh]
        k = k.view(B, S, H, Dh).permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous()
        v = v.view(B, S, H, Dh).permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous()

        # store caches for EMA scoring
        self._last_q = q.detach()
        self._last_k = k.detach()

        # Causal mask base
        device = x.device
        causal = torch.tril(torch.ones(S, S, device=device, dtype=torch.bool))  # [S,S]
        # Attention compute with per-head block compaction following mask
        out = torch.empty_like(q)
        KB = (S + self.block_size - 1) // self.block_size
        if magma_mask is None:
            magma_mask = torch.ones(H, KB, dtype=torch.bool, device=device)
        # Precompute valid key indices per head
        kept_tok_idx = []
        for h in range(H):
            kb_idx = torch.nonzero(magma_mask[h], as_tuple=False).squeeze(-1)
            if kb_idx.numel() == 0:
                kb_idx = torch.tensor([0], device=device)
            tok_idx = (kb_idx[:, None] * self.block_size + torch.arange(self.block_size, device=device)[None, :]).reshape(-1)
            tok_idx = tok_idx[tok_idx < S]
            kept_tok_idx.append(tok_idx)
        # Loop over batch and heads for clarity
        scale = 1.0 / math.sqrt(Dh)
        for b in range(B):
            # key padding mask derived from attn_mask if provided
            if attn_mask is not None:
                valid_len = int(attn_mask[b].sum().item())
            else:
                valid_len = S
            for h in range(H):
                Q = q[b, h, :valid_len, :]  # [Sv,Dh]
                K = k[b, h, kept_tok_idx[h], :]  # [Sk,Dh]
                V = v[b, h, kept_tok_idx[h], :]
                # Restrict K/V further to valid keys
                Kvalid_mask = kept_tok_idx[h] < valid_len
                if Kvalid_mask.sum() == 0:
                    # guarantee at least first key
                    Kvalid_mask = torch.ones_like(kept_tok_idx[h], dtype=torch.bool)
                K = K[Kvalid_mask]
                V = V[Kvalid_mask]
                Sk = K.shape[0]
                # Causal mask on compacted keys: build [Sv,Sk]
                causal_comp = torch.zeros(Q.shape[0], Sk, device=device, dtype=torch.bool)
                # Map each compact key index back to original pos for causal masking
                orig_k_pos = kept_tok_idx[h][Kvalid_mask]
                for qi in range(Q.shape[0]):
                    causal_comp[qi] = orig_k_pos <= qi
                logits = (Q @ K.t()) * scale
                logits = logits.masked_fill(~causal_comp, -1e9)
                attn = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
                O = attn @ V
                # Pad back to S positions
                out_bh = torch.zeros(S, Dh, device=device, dtype=O.dtype)
                out_bh[:Q.shape[0]] = O
                out[b, h] = out_bh
        out = out.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous().view(B, S, D)
        out = self.o_proj(out)
        return out


class TinyTransformer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size: int, d_model: int = 64, n_layers: int = 2,
                 n_heads: int = 4, dim_ff: int = 128, block_size: int = 16,
                 r: int = 8, use_dora: bool = True):
        super().__init__()
        self.vocab_size = vocab_size
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.n_layers = n_layers
        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.block_size = block_size
        self.emb = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)
        self.pos = nn.Embedding(8192, d_model)
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([
            nn.ModuleDict({
                'ln1': nn.LayerNorm(d_model),
                'attn': SelfAttentionMAGMA(d_model, n_heads, block_size=block_size, r=r, use_dora=use_dora),
                'ln2': nn.LayerNorm(d_model),
                'ff': nn.Sequential(
                    nn.Linear(d_model, dim_ff), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(dim_ff, d_model)
                )
            }) for _ in range(n_layers)
        ])
        self.ln_f = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.head = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size)
        self.masks: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None  # [L,H,KB]

    def set_masks(self, M_lh: Optional[torch.Tensor]):
        self.masks = M_lh

    def get_last_qk(self) -> List[Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]]:
        qk = []
        for l in range(self.n_layers):
            attn = self.layers[l]['attn']
            qk.append((attn._last_q, attn._last_k))
        return qk

    def get_head_magnitudes(self) -> Tuple[List[torch.Tensor], List[torch.Tensor]]:
        mQ, mK = [], []
        for l in range(self.n_layers):
            attn = self.layers[l]['attn']
            mQ.append(attn.get_row_norms('q_proj'))
            mK.append(attn.get_row_norms('k_proj'))
        return mQ, mK

    def forward(self, input_ids: torch.Tensor, attention_mask: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None,
                labels: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None):
        # input_ids: [B,S]
        B, S = input_ids.shape
        device = input_ids.device
        pos_ids = torch.arange(S, device=device).unsqueeze(0).expand(B, S)
        x = self.emb(input_ids) + self.pos(pos_ids)
        for l in range(self.n_layers):
            h = self.layers[l]
            x = x + h['attn'](h['ln1'](x), attn_mask=attention_mask,
                               magma_mask=(None if self.masks is None else self.masks[l]))
            x = x + h['ff'](h['ln2'](x))
        x = self.ln_f(x)
        logits = self.head(x)
        loss = None
        if labels is not None:
            # Shifted LM loss; ignore pad token (0)
            loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, logits.size(-1)), labels.view(-1), ignore_index=0)
        return logits, loss

    @torch.no_grad()
    def generate(self, input_ids: torch.Tensor, attention_mask: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None,
                 max_new_tokens: int = 16) -> torch.Tensor:
        self.eval()
        B = input_ids.size(0)
        device = input_ids.device
        out_ids = input_ids.clone()
        for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
            logits, _ = self.forward(out_ids, attention_mask=(out_ids != 0).long())
            next_token = logits[:, -1, :].argmax(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
            out_ids = torch.cat([out_ids, next_token], dim=1)
        return out_ids

@dataclass
class EMATable:
    n_layers: int
    n_heads: int
    n_blocks: int
    decay: float = 0.95

    def __post_init__(self):
        device = 'cpu'
        self.T = torch.zeros(self.n_layers, self.n_heads, self.n_blocks, dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
        self.N = torch.zeros_like(self.T)

    @torch.no_grad()
    def update_layer(self, layer_id: int, head_scores: torch.Tensor):
        # head_scores: [H, KB]
        self.T[layer_id] = self.decay * self.T[layer_id] + (1.0 - self.decay) * head_scores.cpu()
        self.N[layer_id] += 1

    def get_scores(self) -> torch.Tensor:
        return self.T / self.N.clamp_min(1.0)


@torch.no_grad()
def block_scores_from_qk(q: torch.Tensor, k: torch.Tensor,
                         mQ_norm: torch.Tensor, mK_norm: torch.Tensor,
                         block_size: int = 16) -> torch.Tensor:
    # q,k: [B,H,S,D]; mQ_norm,mK_norm: [H]
    qn = torch.linalg.vector_norm(q.float(), dim=-1)  # [B,H,S]
    kn = torch.linalg.vector_norm(k.float(), dim=-1)  # [B,H,S]
    scale = (mQ_norm.to(q.device)[:, None] * mK_norm.to(q.device)[:, None])  # [H,1]
    s = qn * kn * scale  # [B,H,S]
    B, H, S = s.shape
    KB = (S + block_size - 1) // block_size
    pad = KB * block_size - S
    if pad > 0:
        s = F.pad(s, (0, pad))
    s = s.view(B, H, KB, block_size).mean(dim=-1)  # [B,H,KB]
    return s.mean(dim=0).cpu()  # [H,KB]


@torch.no_grad()
def allocate_masks(T_scores: torch.Tensor, rho: float) -> torch.Tensor:
    # T_scores: [L,H,KB]
    L, H, KB = T_scores.shape
    total = L * H * KB
    keep = max(1, int((1.0 - rho) * total))
    flat = T_scores.reshape(-1)
    topk = torch.topk(flat, keep)
    M = torch.zeros_like(flat, dtype=torch.bool)
    M[topk.indices] = True
    M = M.view(L, H, KB)
    # ensure each head keeps at least 1 block
    for l in range(L):
        for h in range(H):
            if not M[l, h].any():
                M[l, h, 0] = True
    return M


@torch.no_grad()
def random_masks_like(T_scores: torch.Tensor, rho: float, seed: int = 0) -> torch.Tensor:
    L, H, KB = T_scores.shape
    rnd = torch.Generator(device=T_scores.device)
    rnd.manual_seed(seed)
    M = torch.rand(L, H, KB, generator=rnd) < (1.0 - rho)
    # ensure at least first block per head
    for l in range(L):
        for h in range(H):
            if not M[l, h].any():
                M[l, h, 0] = True
    return M


class MAGMAController:
    def __init__(self, model: TinyTransformer, seq_len: int, rho_target: float = 0.9,
                 block_size: int = 16, decay: float = 0.95, mask_update_every: int = 50,
                 sparsity_warmup_steps: int = 200):
        self.model = model
        self.seq_len = seq_len
        self.block_size = block_size
        self.KB = (seq_len + block_size - 1) // block_size
        self.ema = EMATable(model.n_layers, model.n_heads, self.KB, decay=decay)
        self.rho_target = rho_target
        self.mask_update_every = mask_update_every
        self.sparsity_warmup_steps = sparsity_warmup_steps
        self.step = 0
        self.M_lh = torch.ones(model.n_layers, model.n_heads, self.KB, dtype=torch.bool)

    def rho_at_step(self) -> float:
        if self.step >= self.sparsity_warmup_steps:
            return self.rho_target
        return 0.7 + (self.rho_target - 0.7) * (self.step / max(1, self.sparsity_warmup_steps))

    @torch.no_grad()
    def update_from_model(self):
        qk_list = self.model.get_last_qk()  # list of (q,k)
        mQ, mK = self.model.get_head_magnitudes()
        for l, (q, k) in enumerate(qk_list):
            if q is None or k is None:
                continue
            head_scores = block_scores_from_qk(q, k, mQ[l], mK[l], block_size=self.block_size)
            self.ema.update_layer(l, head_scores)

    @torch.no_grad()
    def maybe_update_masks(self, use_random: bool = False, rng_seed: int = 0):
        self.step += 1
        if self.step % self.mask_update_every != 0:
            return self.M_lh
        T_scores = self.ema.get_scores()
        rho = self.rho_at_step()
        if use_random:
            self.M_lh = random_masks_like(T_scores, rho, seed=rng_seed)
        else:
            self.M_lh = allocate_masks(T_scores, rho)
        # Apply to model
        self.model.set_masks(self.M_lh.to(next(self.model.parameters()).device))
        return self.M_lh

# Training and eval
